To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the children in this study failed to show match-to-sample relations that were indicative of stimulus equivalence when they were first taught to name all members of a stimulus class, but they showed those relations after they had named the members of the stimulus class.
the development of stimulus equivalence was facilitated by the use of naming.

(a) teaching a child to assign names to stimuli in a functional class may facilitate emergence of stimulus equivalence relations among those stimuli, and (b) teaching a child names for stimuli in an equivalence class may facilitate emergence, without further training, of conditional relations among new stimuli that are related to the named stimuli.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of stimulus equivalence in autistic children.
the role of naming in the development of functional classes, equivalence classes, and conditional relations.
the effects of naming on the development of stimulus relations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
naming may remedial some, but not all, of the failures to develop equivalence classes.
the development of functional and stimulus equivalence classes in autistic children may be facilitated by teaching them names for the members of each class.
naming can facilitate the development of stimulus equivalence in high-functioning, autistic children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
naming is an important factor in the development of stimulus equivalence.
, in the absence of naming, autistic children are unable to develop stimulus equivalence, but naming appears to remediate this deficit in at least some autistic children.

naming is a necessary condition for the emergence of untrained stimulus equivalence relations in some, but not all, subjects, but that it may not be sufficient for the acquisition of new stimulus equivalence classes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the naming of stimuli can be used to facilitate the development of functional classes and stimulus equivalence in high-functioning, autistic preschool children.
, in addition to its role in language, naming may also play a role in the development of stimulus relations.
naming may be important in the development of functional and stimulus equivalence classes.
